newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria resumes democracy talks with Commonwealth.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria resumes democracy talks with Commonwealth.

text.p: Seven Commonwealth ministers began talks with Nigeria's military government in the capital Abuja on Tuesday on speeding up a process to restore democracy and respect human rights, officials said.
A government spokesman said the Commonwealth ministers flew into Abuja on Tuesday and opened the first round of discussions with a Nigerian delegation led by Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi.

On the eve of the talks, the United Nations detailed gross human rights abuses in Africa's most populous nation, which has been in political turmoil since 1993 when the army annulled a presidential vote that would have enthroned democracy.
The U.N. human rights report released in New York said Nigeria's military government has done little to stop summary executions, arbitrary arrests and systematic torture of political prisoners.
The report gave a long list of lawyers, journalists, human rights advocates and politicians it said were killed, arrested without trial, tortured in prison or shot while demonstrating peacefully.
The government-owned Daily Times said Nigeria would insist during the two-day meeting on lifting its suspension from the Commonwealth and stopping all threat of sanctions against it.
Abuja would also demand that the Commonwealth support military ruler General Sani Abacha's plan to restore democracy on October 1, 1998 and begin discussions at the highest level.
The Commonwealth suspended Nigeria last year after it hanged nine minority rights activists, including writer Ken Saro-Wiwa.
It then set up the eight-nation Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG) to push Nigeria towards democracy sooner than detailed by Abacha and to respect human rights.
The two sides met for the first time in May in London where Nigeria insisted that its suspension was unfair and that until this issue is settled there can be no progress on other matters.
The chairmen of five political parties recently registered to contest for power under Abacha's transition programme met in Abuja on Monday and are expected to address the CMAG.
"They will tell the Commonwealth that the transition programme is on course," said a foreign ministry source.
The CMAG team is without Canada which has taken a hard line against Nigeria's military government on the twin issues of rights abuses and democracy.
CMAG at first agreed a set of sanctions against Nigeria but later decided to hold off their imposition to keep the dialogue going by sending a fact-finding mission.
Nigeria refused to allow a fact-finding mission, saying the United Nations had undertaken a similar assignment.

The 53-nation Commonwealth groups mainly Britain and its former colonies. CMAG is made up of foreign ministers of Britain, Canada, New Zealand, South Africa, Zimbabwe, Ghana, Jamaica and Malaysia and its report will be submitted to the Commonwealth secretariat in London.
Nigeria's opposition appealed in an open memorandum to the Commonwealth ministers to press for the release of political detainees during the Abuja talks.
It sought especially that pressure be applied on Abacha to free Moshood Abiola, a wealthy businessman presumed to have won the annulled 1993 presidential election.

Abiola has been detained since 1994 when he defied the military government and proclaimed himself president on the basis of the 1993 vote. Many of his supporters are also detained or have fled into exile in Britain and the United States.
The Commonwealth says military ruler General Sani Abacha's timetable to hand over to an elected president by October 1998 is too long and wants it before next year's Commonwealth summit.
The government insists the programme is on course and will not be changed because of pressure from abroad.
Abacha seized power in the chaos that followed annulment of the 1993 presidential poll by a previous military government.
